n0001.title: Spider Silk
n0001.gist: Spider silk is a uniquely tough, adhesive protein fibre whose structure and production methods researchers are now trying to replicate artificially.
n0001.question: Spider silk — what makes it so mechanically exceptional and how might humans reproduce it? (an overview across biology and engineering)

n0002.title: Spider Silk
n0002.gist: Spiders spin silk for many purposes—trapping prey, courtship signalling, and protection—making it one of the most versatile materials found in nature.
n0002.question: Spider silk — why do spiders produce it and what roles does it serve beyond web-building? (a general overview)

n0003.title: What silk is used for
n0003.gist: Spiders use silk not just for webs but for sensing, trapping, nesting and even mating signals, varying the fibre's thickness and stickiness by purpose.

n0009.title: Collecting silk
n0009.gist: Because forcing silk from a single spider is possible but harvesting it at scale from many spiders is far harder than farming silkworms, bulk production remains difficult.

n0011.title: Silk and mating
n0011.gist: All spiders make silk, and it carries courtship signals and pheromones between sexes, though why males themselves sometimes spin silk during mating is still poorly understood.

n0013.title: Properties
n0013.gist: Spider silk's layered molecular architecture gives rise to mechanical and adhesive properties that outperform many engineered materials.
n0013.question: Properties — why is spider silk stronger and tougher than comparable man-made fibres? (structural, mechanical and adhesive evidence)

n0014.title: Structural
n0014.gist: Silk's strength comes from a layered structure where hard crystal-like sheets sit inside a stretchy amorphous matrix, with added chemicals guarding against moisture loss, fungi and bacteria.

n0022.title: Mechanical
n0022.gist: Dragline silk combines strength and stretchiness to absorb more energy before breaking than steel or Kevlar, with specific properties like stiffness, tensile strength, density, toughness and heat tolerance all measured and compared across spider species.

n0049.title: Adhesive
n0049.gist: Silk's sticky attachment discs are made from a two-part secretion that hardens instantly, stays biodegradable, and bonds reliably to many different surfaces in nature.

n0052.title: Uses
n0052.gist: A single spider can spin up to seven silk types, each suited to a different task such as capturing prey, reproducing, travelling, or sensing danger.
n0052.question: Uses — how does silk's variety let spiders perform so many different ecological functions? (a table of uses)

n0056.title: Silk types
n0056.gist: Different glands produce chemically distinct silks—dragline, capture-spiral, egg-sac, wrapping and glue types—each engineered for a specific structural or adhesive role in the web.
n0056.question: Silk types — how do different glands produce silks tailored to different jobs? (two comparison tables)

n0066.title: Synthesis and fibre spinning
n0066.gist: Spiders convert liquid protein stored in glands into solid fibre on demand by pulling it through a tapering duct that changes its chemistry and molecular alignment as it goes.
n0066.question: Synthesis and fibre spinning — how does a spider turn liquid protein into solid silk thread? (a gland-by-gland mechanism)

n0067.title: Spinning process
n0067.gist: Despite its name, silk "spinning" involves no rotation; it is a pulling process called pultrusion in which fibre is drawn out through one or more internal glands.

n0072.title: Silk gland
n0072.gist: Inside the spinneret, silk protein moves through a secretory tail, storage sac, funnel and tapering duct where shear force, acidity and water removal convert liquid protein into solid aligned fibre.

n0092.title: Artificial synthesis
n0092.gist: Scientists have tried to recreate both spider silk's feedstock and its spinning conditions using bacteria, goats, plants and mechanical devices, but synthetic fibres still fall short of the natural material.
n0092.question: Artificial synthesis — why has it been so hard to manufacture silk as strong as a real spider's? (several engineering approaches)

n0093.title: Feedstock
n0093.gist: Replicating silk's long, complex protein molecule requires extracting it from genetically engineered organisms such as bacteria, silkworms or goats before it can be purified and spun.

n0100.title: Geometry
n0100.gist: Because feedstock alone is not enough, researchers must also mimic the spider's duct geometry using methods like syringes, superhydrophobic surfaces, microfluidics and electrospinning.

n0114.title: Other shapes
n0114.gist: Beyond fibres, silk proteins can self-assemble into capsules, sheets, nanowires and membranes useful for drug delivery, wound healing and tissue engineering.

n0117.title: Synthetic spider silk
n0117.gist: Despite progress using bacteria, yeast, plants and animals to produce silk-like proteins, synthetic fibres remain thicker, weaker and less flexible than natural dragline silk, though companies and labs keep narrowing the gap.

n0130.title: Research
n0130.gist: A timeline of landmark studies traces how scientists gradually worked out silk's chemistry, gene sequence, structure, and spinning behaviour over six decades.
n0130.question: Research — which studies built up today's understanding of spider silk? (a chronological table of key papers)

n0133.title: Human uses
n0133.gist: Beyond webs, people have tried for centuries to turn spider silk into fabric and have since applied it to medicine, optics and advanced technology.
n0133.question: Human uses — what practical purposes has spider silk served throughout history? (historical and modern examples)

n0134.title: Early textile attempts
n0134.gist: Early inventors Bon and Termeyer tried weaving and reeling spider silk centuries ago, but neither succeeded in producing it in commercially useful quantities, a limit modern projects still struggle with.

n0139.title: Medicine
n0139.gist: Folk remedies once used spider silk tubes to dress wounds, likely because the silk has antiseptic properties and contains vitamin K, and modern research has tested it for nerve regeneration.

n0142.title: Science and technology
n0142.gist: Spider silk's fineness and strength have made it useful as crosshairs in optical instruments, in diffraction experiments, biolenses, and even as a support thread for laser fusion targets.
